title: Tropical Pitcher Plants ( Nepenthes spp.): Indoor Care, Growing Tips, & Plant Guide

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plants Facts at a Glance
paragraphs.text: Botanical Name: Nepenthes spp. Common Name: Tropical pitcher plant Plant Type: Indoor; carnivorous perennial Mature Size: Typically, 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide Best Soil: 60% sphagnum moss, 20% perlite, 20% orchid bark Light Level: Bright indirect light Humidity: above 60% Watering: Keep moist; do not allow plants to dry out Temperatures:

paragraphs.heading: Lowland species 70°F to 95°F
paragraphs.text: Highland species 70°F and 80°F, with a drop to 50°F to 60°F at night

paragraphs.heading: Lowland species 70°F to 95°F
paragraphs.text: Pet Safe: Yes Indoor Plant Difficulty Level: Novice to experienced grower

paragraphs.heading: How Tropical Pitcher Plants Catch Insects
paragraphs.text: The pitchers lure insects in with fragrance, color, and an intoxicating nectar. Once an insect loses its foothold, it will fall into a pitcher that is divided into two zones.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Flowers
paragraphs.text: The plants are dioecious, meaning that male or female flowers are produced on separate plants. 70% of wild plants are male.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Flowers
paragraphs.text: The flowers are produced on a stalk that grows above both sets of pitchers.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Flowers
paragraphs.text: Dozens to hundreds of densely packed small flowers are produced on a raceme inflorescence.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Flowers
paragraphs.text: Some species produce colorful flowers, but the majority are pale green. The scent varies among the species as well.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Flowers
paragraphs.text: Some flowers offer a sweet scent, while others smell like cat urine. Flower scents developed to attract different pollinators.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Light Requirements
paragraphs.text: Most tropical pitcher plants like bright, diffused light and can tolerate a few hours of direct sun in the morning or late afternoon.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Light Requirements
paragraphs.text: Locate near an east or west-facing window.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Watering and Humidity Needs
paragraphs.text: Plants can be sensitive to tap water; it is better to use rainwater or distilled water when possible.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Watering and Humidity Needs
paragraphs.text: Provide plants with humidity levels above 60%.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Watering and Humidity Needs
paragraphs.text: For more information about watering indoor plants, visit Indoor Plants – Watering (HGIC 1459) .

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Watering and Humidity Needs
paragraphs.text: If plants are not producing pitchers, low light and low humidity levels are usually the reason.

paragraphs.text: Highland species prefer warm daytime temperatures and cool nights.

paragraphs.heading: Fertilizing Tropical Pitcher Plants
paragraphs.text: If insects are not provided, plants can be fertilized with an organic fertilizer twice a month during the growing season.

paragraphs.heading: Kelp extract
paragraphs.text: Dilute the fertilizer to ¼ to of the recommended strength.

paragraphs.heading: Kelp extract
paragraphs.text: Apply the fertilizer to the leaves and open pitchers.

paragraphs.heading: Repotting Tropical Pitcher Plants
paragraphs.text: Repot plants every 2 to 3 years.

paragraphs.heading: Potting medium breaks down
paragraphs.text: Remove old or brown pitchers.

paragraphs.heading: Potting medium breaks down
paragraphs.text: Use water to dislodge old potting medium, if necessary.

paragraphs.heading: Potting medium breaks down
paragraphs.text: Replant into a slightly larger container.

paragraphs.heading: Best Soil for Tropical Pitcher Plants
paragraphs.text: Use a light, low-nutrient potting medium that retains moisture.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitchers Turning Brown or Black
paragraphs.text: An individual pitcher will turn brown or black as its lifespan comes to an end.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitchers Turning Brown or Black
paragraphs.text: A sudden change in the environment can cause multiple older pitchers to dry out.

paragraphs.heading: Tropical Pitcher Plant Pests
paragraphs.text: Aphids, mealybugs, thrips, and scale insects can be problematic.

paragraphs.heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Tropical Pitcher Plants
paragraphs.text: Why isn't my tropical pitcher plant making pitchers? Low light and low humidity are the most common causes.

paragraphs.heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Tropical Pitcher Plants
paragraphs.text: Do tropical pitcher plants need fertilizer? Plants can be fed insects or fertilized with diluted organic fertilizer during the growing season.
